evals.name: collect-filter-bandwidth-cost
evals.prompt: In a Convex query I write `const recent = (await ctx.db.query("events").collect()).filter(e => e.userId === uid)`. The table has ~50k rows but only a few match. A teammate says "it's fine, .filter throws away the rows we don't need so they don't cost anything." Is that right? What's the correct approach?
evals.expected_output: No. EVERY row returned by .collect() counts toward database bandwidth, including the ones the later .filter() discards — the filter runs in JS after all 50k rows were read. Worse, because the query read all those rows, any change to ANY of them re-runs the query (or conflicts a mutation). .collect() should only be used for small (<~1000) result sets. Fix: add an index `by_user` on userId and do `ctx.db.query("events").withIndex("by_user", q => q.eq("userId", uid))` so only matching rows are read; or .paginate()/.take(n) for large browses.
evals.truth: WRONG — all .collect() rows count toward bandwidth even ones .filter drops, and reading them re-runs/conflicts on any change; use withIndex (by_user) to read only matches, or paginate/take; .collect only for <~1000

evals.name: date-now-in-query-cache
evals.prompt: My Convex query lists currently-released movies: `ctx.db.query("movies").withIndex("by_released_at", q => q.lte("releasedAt", Date.now())).collect()`. Clients complain the list is sometimes stale and the query seems to re-run constantly. What's the underlying problem and the right fix?
evals.expected_output: Calling Date.now() inside a query is the problem. Convex queries are cached and only re-run when their underlying DATA changes, not when the wall clock advances — so the Date.now() bound is frozen at the value from the last data-driven execution, giving stale results; and the time value also makes the cache invalidate more than necessary. Fix: don't read the clock in the query. Add an `isReleased` boolean updated by a scheduled function and query `.withIndex("by_is_released", q => q.eq("isReleased", true))`; or pass the current time from the client as an argument, rounded (e.g. to the minute) to limit cache churn.
evals.truth: Date.now() in a query is the bug — query only re-runs on DATA change so the time goes stale + over-invalidates cache; fix = scheduled fn sets an isReleased boolean to index, or pass a rounded client timestamp as an arg

evals.name: runaction-same-runtime-overhead
evals.prompt: Inside a Convex action I have `await ctx.runAction(internal.scrape.scrapeSinglePage, { url })`, and scrapeSinglePage is a normal action in the same file (no "use node"). Reviewer flagged it. Why, and what should it be?
evals.expected_output: ctx.runAction is a full extra Convex function call with its own memory and CPU allocation and overhead — it's not a cheap function call. When the target runs in the SAME runtime it should just be a plain TypeScript function call, not runAction. Refactor scrapeSinglePage into a plain async helper `scrapeSinglePage(ctx, { url })` and call it directly. runAction is only justified when you must cross into a different runtime — e.g. calling a Node.js ("use node") action from the default runtime.
evals.truth: runAction = extra function call with its own memory/CPU overhead; same runtime → call a plain TS helper directly; reserve runAction only for crossing into a different (Node) runtime

evals.name: sequential-runquery-transaction-consistency
evals.prompt: In a Convex action I do `const team = await ctx.runQuery(api.teams.get, { id }); const owner = await ctx.runQuery(api.users.get, { id: team.ownerId });`. Besides being two round-trips, is there a correctness problem with reading the team and its owner this way?
evals.expected_output: Yes — consistency. Each ctx.runQuery (and ctx.runMutation) runs in its OWN separate transaction. So the team read and the owner read are not a consistent snapshot: the data can change between the two calls, and team/owner may not agree with each other. Fix: do both reads inside a SINGLE query that returns them together (e.g. getTeamAndOwner) so they come from one consistent transaction. (Same idea for writes: batch a loop of per-item mutations into one mutation like insertUsers(users[]).)
evals.truth: each ctx.runQuery/runMutation runs in its OWN transaction so the two reads aren't a consistent snapshot (can disagree); combine into ONE query (getTeamAndOwner) / batch writes into one mutation

evals.name: redundant-prefix-index
evals.prompt: My Convex schema has `.index("by_org", ["orgId"]).index("by_org_and_status", ["orgId", "status"])`. I query sometimes by org alone and sometimes by org+status. Do I need both indexes?
evals.expected_output: Usually no — by_org is prefix-redundant with by_org_and_status. A compound index can serve a query on its leading field(s), so for an org-only query you use by_org_and_status and simply omit the status condition: `.withIndex("by_org_and_status", q => q.eq("orgId", orgId))`. Drop by_org. Fewer indexes means less storage and lower write overhead on every insert/update. The one reason to keep both is if you need a different sort order that the compound index can't provide (e.g. ordering org rows by plain _creationTime).
evals.truth: Drop by_org — it's a redundant prefix of by_org_and_status; query the compound index and omit the trailing status eq; fewer indexes = less storage + write overhead; keep both only if a different sort order is needed

evals.name: public-cron-target-internal
evals.prompt: I scheduled a daily cron: `crons.daily("digest", { hourUTC: 9, minuteUTC: 0 }, api.messages.sendDigest, {})`, where sendDigest is exported as a normal `mutation`. It works, but is there a security concern with how it's wired?
evals.expected_output: Yes. sendDigest is a PUBLIC function (exported via mutation and referenced as api.messages.sendDigest), so it's callable by anyone on the internet, not just your cron — they can trigger digests at will. Functions only ever called from within Convex (crons, schedulers, ctx.run*) should be marked INTERNAL (internalMutation) and referenced via internal.* . Fix: make it internalMutation and schedule internal.messages.sendDigest. Convex guarantees internal functions can't be invoked from outside, so it's safe (and you can relax the public-input checks).
evals.truth: sendDigest is public (api.*) so anyone can call it; cron/scheduler/ctx.run* targets must be internal — convert to internalMutation and reference internal.messages.sendDigest

evals.name: filter-paginate-exception
evals.prompt: I keep reading "never use .filter on a Convex query." But I have a paginated feed and want to drop hidden posts: `ctx.db.query("posts").withIndex("by_channel", q => q.eq("channel", c)).filter(q => q.eq(q.field("hidden"), false)).paginate(opts)`. Is using .filter here actually wrong?
evals.expected_output: No — this is the documented exception. .filter on a .paginate() query is acceptable, because a filtered paginated query still returns the requested page-size number of documents (Convex keeps reading to fill the page), so you don't get short/empty pages. The general 'avoid .filter' rule is about non-paginated reads where .filter scans and bills every matched row; with pagination the filter is fine. (If hidden-ness is a common, selective query, an index that includes it could still be better, but .filter here is not a violation.)
evals.truth: Not wrong — .filter on a .paginate() query is the explicit exception (filtered page still returns the requested document count); the avoid-.filter rule targets non-paginated reads

evals.name: access-control-userid-arg
evals.prompt: A public Convex mutation updates a user's profile and takes `args: { userId: v.id("users"), bio: v.string() }`, then patches that userId. It has argument validators, so it's validated. Is it secure? How should authorization work?
evals.expected_output: No — validators check the SHAPE of input but not WHO is calling. Accepting userId as an argument and trusting it for authorization is spoofable: any caller can pass someone else's id and edit their profile. Public functions must derive identity server-side from ctx.auth.getUserIdentity() (null if signed out), and use that identity (e.g. tokenIdentifier) to decide what the caller may touch — never authorize off a userId/email passed in args. So: look up the caller via getUserIdentity, and only allow patching their own profile (or check a role). Factor the check into a reusable helper.
evals.truth: Not secure — validators check shape not identity; a userId arg is spoofable; derive the caller from ctx.auth.getUserIdentity() server-side and authorize on that, never on a userId/email passed as an argument
